SOAH DOCKET NO. 473-26-16349  |  PUC DOCKET NO. 59475
SOAH DOCKET NO. 473-26-10397  |  PUC DOCKET NO. 59182
Whether Import Path 2 is needed
Susan Burrow’s Reply Brief on Remand
Preliminary Order Issues 11 and 13
Table of Contents
I Argument	2
A The companies’ own witness says the rules changed	2
B The companies must show why Path 2 is needed	3
C Someone must take responsibility for the engineering	4
D Get clear answers about the engineering rules	5
E Statewide savings do not prove savings from Path 2	5
II Proposed findings of fact	6
III Proposed conclusions of law	7
What I ask the ALJs to do	7
Certificate of Service	8
TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:
Oncor and LCRA have not proven that Import Path 2 is needed. The ALJs should keep their recommendation to deny the applications in Dockets 59475 and 59182. The companies want permission to build these lines. They must prove why the lines are needed. Pointing to a bigger plan and predictions of future electricity use does not finish that job.
The issue is straightforward: the companies have not shown why this path is necessary when the future electricity use behind their studies is still uncertain. It is not the public's responsibility to prove that the whole Permian Basin Reliability Plan is wrong. The companies must prove the need for the lines in these applications. They have not done so, and the applications should be denied.
I Argument
A The companies’ own witness says the rules changed
The companies’ own witness, Jared Gurley, explains that the rules changed. In his May 28, 2026 testimony, he describes how HB 5066 changed the way future electricity use is considered. The new approach includes customers who have not signed an agreement to connect to the grid. That is a major difference in the information going into the studies.
The new approach says those possible customers must be considered. However, it does not say that they will all show up, or whether they will use the amount of power requested by the date assumed. Past growth does not prove every new prediction. The companies still have to show that the expected electricity use supports the need for this path.
B The companies must show why Path 2 is needed
The Permian Basin plan used 23,659 megawatts of electricity demand for 2030 and 26,400 megawatts for 2038. These are the amounts put into the computer studies. They do not, by themselves, prove how much power customers will actually need by those dates or why Import Path 2 is the necessary answer.
The companies point to studies that lowered expected electricity use and still found similar major grid problems. Gurley says the 2024 Regional Transmission Plan used only 27.6 percent of the utilities’ predicted demand. That plan also tested a reduction in demand supported by utility officers’ letters from over 31,000 megawatts to less than 16,000. The 2025 plan tested removing that kind of demand altogether, from over 23,000 megawatts to zero. Those results deserve attention. But the studies also changed assumptions about power plants. They are not a simple recheck of the Permian Basin plan with only demand changed, and they do not automatically show why Path 2 itself is needed.
The companies must connect the dots. Which customers are expected to need power? How far along are their projects? When will they connect? What grid problem will remain after other planned lines and supported power-plant additions are counted? Why does that remaining problem require Path 2? A study of the wider grid can answer those questions. The companies do not have to study every line by itself, but they do have to point to evidence that proves their case.
The later computer studies started with the proposed lines already included. The 2024 plan included all three Permian import paths. The 2025 plan included the whole statewide 765-kilovolt expansion plan in its starting cases for 2030 and 2031. Starting with the lines in place can help planners test the larger system. but it does not, by itself, prove that each line has to be built.
Gurley acknowledges that a December 2024 scheduling spreadsheet put the need for the three paths in 2038. He says later work showed they were needed by 2030. Moving the date forward eight years requires a clear explanation backed by the study results. A new date is not proof simply because the companies now use that date.
Landowners are not required to pay for their own computer study to make the companies prove their case. The responsibility to prove need stays with the companies.
C Someone must take responsibility for the engineering
ERCOT, the Texas grid operator, used engineering to study the grid and recommend new lines. Gurley describes overloaded equipment, voltage problems, and trouble moving power through the system. One of the companies’ reports calls part of the work “ERCOT Engineering Studies.” Texas law includes this kind of technical study and planning in its definition of engineering. Calling the finished report a plan does not change the work behind it.
The national reliability rules also show why this work calls for engineering judgment. NERC Standard TPL-001-5.1 requires computer models, yearly reviews, and written explanations of the assumptions and results. It calls for testing changes in electricity use, power plants, power transfers, and the dates new lines will be ready. Related Modeling on Demand rules cover the information used in the models and checks on model accuracy. These rules help explain the work. They do not decide which Texas licensing exceptions apply.
Using national reliability rules does not automatically make a study a complete yearly review under those rules. It also does not prove that every possible customer is ready to connect. Naming a national standard cannot replace proof of why Path 2 is needed.
Tom Green, a licensed engineer, raised a concern in his testimony: Who is the engineer responsible for the Permian Basin report, and where is the signed engineering document showing that responsibility? His concern deserves an answer. His testimony alone does not prove that ERCOT broke a licensing rule or that no engineer supervised the work.
The Texas engineering board has explained a similar point about transportation planning. Collecting general information is different from using engineering judgment to recommend specific facilities. Although that guidance is about transportation, not ERCOT, it still supports looking at what the work actually involved instead of treating the word “plan” as an answer.
D Get clear answers about the engineering rules
There are several different questions here: whether the work is engineering, whether the business must be registered, who must hold an engineer’s license, and which finished documents must be signed and sealed. The companies should identify who took professional responsibility for the reports and which rules apply. Any claimed exception must comply with the law and the facts. It should not be assumed just because ERCOT prepared the work.
An engineer’s seal identifies professional responsibility for covered work. It does not prove the need for a transmission line. The ALJs should address responsibility for the studies and the proof of need as separate questions. Neither one answers the other.
I ask the ALJs to address what these studies actually prove and who is professionally responsible for the work. I also ask them to request, or recommend that the Commission request, a written answer from the Texas Board of Professional Engineers and Land Surveyors about the registration and sealing rules that apply to these reports. Section 1001.601 provides that process. Section 1001.553 requires public officials to report a violation that has been established. I am asking for the proper board review, not asking the ALJs to take over the Board’s enforcement job.
The Commission must deal with the important evidence. Its rules require specific written reasons and a legal basis for changing the ALJs’ findings or legal conclusions. The companies’ missing proof cannot be substituted by an endorsement. These duties belong to the Commission as a whole; a Commissioner’s engineering license alone does not prove personal wrongdoing.
E Statewide savings do not prove savings from Path 2
Issue 13 asks how much customers would save because these lines ease limits on moving electricity. The companies cite savings for much larger statewide plans. Those figures do not tell us Path 2’s share. The cost to produce power, the amount customers pay for power, and a market measure called congestion rent are different things. The companies’ statement that a reliability project does not have to pass an economic test does not provide the missing dollar estimate. The ALJs should say plainly that the cited evidence does not establish that estimate. That does not mean the savings are zero; it means the amount has not been proven.
SOAH Order No. 35 does not allow parties to add new evidence through their briefs. And likewise, information available to the public is not automatically evidence in this case. Any new evidence requires permission under the proper procedures and a fair chance for the parties to respond. The ALJs should decide the applications on the evidence before them, which does not establish the need for Path 2.
II Proposed findings of fact
1. Gurley explains that HB 5066 changed planning to include possible customers who have not signed agreements to connect to the grid.
2. The Permian Basin plan put electricity demand of 23,659 megawatts for 2030 and 26,400 megawatts for 2038 into its studies.
3. The later studies started with the three Permian import paths or the whole STEP plan already included. That starting point alone does not prove that each part is necessary.
4. Studies that tested lower electricity use still found similar major grid problems. They also changed assumptions about power plants. Those results must be read with the actual study conditions in mind.
5. Gurley acknowledges that the scheduling spreadsheet listed 2038 and says later work supports a 2030 need date.
6. Green raises a concern about who took professional responsibility for the Permian Basin report. A look into a licensing violation, a lack of business registration, or a lack of engineering supervision should be conducted.
7. The cited statewide savings figures do not establish how much customers would save from fewer power-transfer limits because of Path 2. The amount has not been proven. That is different from saying it is zero.
8. Taken together, the studies, the tests using lower electricity demand, and the testimony do not prove that these Path 2 facilities are needed to meet state or federal reliability standards. The ALJs should make that finding.
III Proposed conclusions of law
1. The companies must prove that their applications meet the law. The requirement to consider future customers does not require the ALJs to accept predictions without adequate support.
2. The rule giving weight to ERCOT’s recommendation does not make approval automatic. The companies still have to prove need.
3. Texas law covers engineering studies and planning. The rules for business registration, individual licenses, and signed and sealed documents must be applied to the actual work and any applicable exceptions.
4. The Texas engineering board has a process for giving a written answer about how its law applies. Public officials must report an established violation. That does not give the ALJs the Board’s enforcement powers.
5. The decision must be based on evidence properly placed before the decision-makers. Changing the ALJs’ findings or legal conclusions requires the written reasons and legal basis required by the Commission’s rules.
6. The companies have not proven the need required for these certificates. The applications should be denied. The separate questions about engineering responsibility do not excuse that failure of proof.
What I ask the ALJs to do
I ask the ALJs to maintain their recommendation to deny both applications. For Issue 11, they should find that the companies have not proven these lines are needed to meet state or federal reliability standards. For Issue 13, they should find that the cited evidence does not establish a separate estimate of customer savings from easing power-transfer limits through Path 2. They should also address who took professional responsibility for the studies and request the Board review described above.
The companies are asking for permission to build lines across private property across the state, and charge customers for them. They must prove why these lines are necessary. A larger plan, changing predictions, and statewide savings figures do not fill the gaps in their proof. The applications in Dockets 59475 and 59182 should be denied.
Respectfully submitted,

/s/ Susan Burrow

Salado, TX 76571
